report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is not false, but it is overstated if presented as a universal rule. The best available evidence suggests that *improving bedroom ventilation*—which opening a window or door can accomplish—can modestly improve measured and perceived sleep quality. It does not establish that an open window/door itself will improve sleep for everyone or in every setting.

A randomized controlled field study found that experimentally improving bedroom air quality lowered CO₂ and significantly improved actigraphy-based sleep measures, perceived air freshness, next-day sleepiness, concentration, and logical-thinking performance. This supports a causal effect of ventilation/air quality, rather than merely an association.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168/

A later two-week field intervention in 40 Danish bedrooms reported lower CO₂, VOCs and PM₁₀ with an open window, alongside improved objectively measured and self-rated sleep. That is direct evidence consistent with the claim, though the result combines window-opening with environmental changes such as temperature and outdoor-air exposure.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322008605

Earlier research specifically examining window/door opening involved only 17 healthy young adults, so generalizability—to older adults, people with insomnia, noisy/polluted areas, or different climates—is limited.  
https://research.tue.nl/en/publications/windowdoor-opening-mediated-bedroom-ventilation-and-its-impact-on/

A review characterizes the evidence linking bedroom air quality and sleep as limited. Thus, it is premature to treat opening a window or door as a proven general sleep intervention.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132320306004

Practical takeaway: if a room is stuffy or poorly ventilated, improving ventilation may help; but an open window can also introduce noise, light, allergens, smoke/pollution, or uncomfortable temperatures that worsen sleep.
